data.title: Meduza: Moscow high society: celebrities pose for photos in front of giant ‘STALIN’ sign. Scenes from the premiere of a new Russian miniseries about the Soviet dictator.
data.summary: Director Vladimir Bortko has made a six-part feature film called Stalin. The first episodes will premiere on the Kion streaming service on November 26, with a television premiere on REN TV set for December 6. Bortko reportedly worked on the project for 15 years, and the script is based on declassified documents and memoirs. The story takes place between 1945 and 1953, the year Joseph Stalin died. The filmmakers promise to show “not good or bad, but the truth,” but judging by the trailer, it’s a typical Russian “patriotic blockbuster” in which a resolute leader stands up to the West. Stalin is played by Igor Mirkurbanov, an actor who has mostly played antiheroes onstage, including the Pretender in Boris Godunov and the elder Karamazov in The Karamazovs. The film also stars Viktor Sukhorukov as Khrushchev and Alexander Yatsko as Beria. On November 23, a society premiere of the film was held at Moscow’s Khudozhestvenny movie theater, where invited Russian celebrities posed for photos in front of a press wall bearing the word “STALIN.” Take a look at these photos.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/11/26/.label: Meduza: Moscow high society: celebrities pose for photos in front of giant ‘STALIN’ sign. Scenes from the premiere of a new Russian miniseries about the Soviet dictator.

data.title: Meduza: ‘No reports, no strikes’: Russia’s pro-war bloggers slam proposed prison sentences for sharing photos and videos of Ukrainian attacks
data.summary: Yesterday, a group of Russian senators introduced a bill in the State Duma that calls for prison terms of up to five years for illegally distributing information about the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes, as well as terrorist attacks and sabotage. Bans on publishing photos and videos of attack aftermath are already in effect in many regions, though until now the punishment has only involved administrative fines. Now a new article could appear in the Criminal Code as well. Authors of pro-war Z-channels and “military correspondents” reacted to the initiative with unanimous criticism. In their view, almost anything could be classified as illegal distribution, and the bill is aimed at eliminating “unnecessary questions” about how the state allowed this to happen. The Kremlin, however, said that “there is a war going on, and accordingly, the decisions that need to be made during wartime must be made to ensure security.” We present a short collection of Z-bloggers’ opinions on the new bill.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/11/27/.label: Meduza: ‘No reports, no strikes’: Russia’s pro-war bloggers slam proposed prison sentences for sharing photos and videos of Ukrainian attacks

data.title: Meduza: How Russian soldiers are escaping Putin’s war. Five deserters recount their journeys across borders, through forests with bears, and over the English Channel.
data.summary: It is well known that some Russians manage to successfully desert: flee straight from the front and then illegally cross the border. But how exactly does this happen? How do people decide to take such a risk, how do they get out of the country, and what harsh reality do they face after managing to leave Russia? We recorded several stories of successful escapes. Meduza found everyone featured in this story through the project Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), which helped them escape. It was launched in 2022 by Grigory Sverdlin, former director of Nochlezhka, Russia’s oldest organization helping homeless people. Sverdlin’s book, Punkt Obogreva (“Warming Station”), was recently published by Meduza’s publishing house.

https://meduza.io/en/feature/2026/11/27/.label: Meduza: How Russian soldiers are escaping Putin’s war. Five deserters recount their journeys across borders, through forests with bears, and over the English Channel.
